answer: The land was Ottoman for about 400 years and never one province: the south was the district of Jerusalem, the north split between the provinces of Beirut and Syria, and no province was named Palestine. Britain took Jerusalem in December 1917. The Balfour Declaration favoured a Jewish national home and said nothing should prejudice the 'civil and religious rights' of other communities, without mentioning political rights. The 1922 Mandate recited the Jewish people's historical connection to the land, recognised a Jewish agency (the Zionist Organisation) as a public body, and in Article 6 told Britain to facilitate Jewish immigration and encourage close settlement, including on state lands, 'while ensuring' other sections' rights were not prejudiced. Transjordan was excluded from the national-home clauses. The 1939 White Paper limited Jewish immigration. Whether McMahon's 1915 offer of Arab independence left Palestine out is disputed. Rule lay with the Ottomans, then Britain as Mandatory.

facts.text: Under Ottoman rule no province was named Palestine. The south was the independent sanjak (Mutasarrifate) of Jerusalem, answering directly to Istanbul; the north belonged to the vilayet of Beirut (the sanjaks of Acre and Nablus) and, before 1888, to the vilayet of Syria (Damascus).

Whether that left Palestine out is disputed (see contested).

contested.text: Whether McMahon's 1915 promise covered Palestine is disputed. The British government's 1939 White Paper held that the whole of Palestine west of the Jordan was excluded from the pledge. But the 1939 committee report records that the British representatives themselves told the Arab side that its case 'has greater force than has appeared hitherto' and that the language of exclusion was 'not so specific and unmistakable as it was thought to be at the time', while still maintaining that on a proper construction Palestine was excluded. The Arab representatives argued that Palestine was in fact and in intention included in the area of promised Arab independence, and that reading 'district' as 'vilayet' was untenable. A 2011 Commonweal review of a book by Jonathan Schneer notes it has been argued that the Arabic translation led Hussein to read 'districts' more widely; that line is a reviewer's summary, not a historian's own words. Historians still differ; this card reports the dispute, not a verdict.

contested.text: Whether Britain's wartime promises were consistent is contested. The Imperial War Museums say Britain had already promised Palestine to the Arabs as an independent state and promised France an internationally administered zone before it signed the Balfour Declaration. Israel's Foreign Ministry reads the Declaration, and its inclusion in the Mandate, as international recognition of the Jewish people's right to self-determination in its historical homeland.

sources.title: The Balfour Declaration
sources.quote: The Declaration expressed the British government's recognition of and support for the inalienable right of the Jewish people for self-determination in their historical homeland

could_not_verify: Britannica's pages on Ottoman Palestine and the Balfour Declaration would not load, so they are not cited.
The Palestine Royal Commission report (1937) states the Ottoman divisions and the McMahon dispute, but I could not read a copy from this machine, so it is not cited.
The exact date the Ottomans took the region (1516-17) is not on any page I could read for this card; the card says 'about 400 years' instead.
I did not find a readable page by a historian who argues the Arab reading of McMahon's letter in his own words; the Arab case is quoted from the British 1939 committee report and a magazine summary.
Three sources from three different sites for the Ottoman districts: the fourth (a UN committee study) is labelled government and does not count.
The Palquest and Library of Congress copies of the Transjordan resolution returned http 403 here; fact 8 rests on the League's own note (an ECF-hosted scan), the UN committee report and COJS instead.

The Mandate facts (5 to 8, 10, 11) are record facts: the record is the League's Mandate text on UNISPAL. The two confirming sources (UN committee report, Survey of Palestine, Anglo-American Committee appendix, COJS excerpt) either reproduce or paraphrase that same text, so they check our reading of it; they are not independent measurements of anything.

Round two reviewer: facts 5, 6, 7, 10 and 11 (Mandate) have only one source that restates the text in its own words (the UN committee report for Articles 2, 4 (a block quotation), 6 and 25; the Anglo-American Committee for the preamble); the other confirming source in each is a reprint of the Mandate's text (COJS excerpt, Survey of Palestine appendix), which is a copy and not a reader.
not_claimed: This card does not say Palestine was empty or that no people with a claim lived there before 1917; chapter 2's population card gives the counts.
It does not say the Balfour Declaration or the Mandate settled who owned the land or created a right of the Jewish people over the Arabs of Palestine.
It does not say Britain kept its promises to either side.
It does not say the White Paper stopped Jewish immigration entirely; it set a quota.

skeptic.notes: Round two, after the record rule. Read every is_record source (Balfour on Avalon, McMahon letter, Mandate text on UNISPAL, ECF scan of the League note, White Paper on Avalon) and compared each record fact's wording with it: all eight are worded as what the record says, and Articles 4 and 6 are quoted correctly. Fixed from round one: the British concession is quoted from the 1939 report itself; Articles 4 and 6 are on the card; fact 8 quote is complete. [must-fix] Readers are not real readers for five record facts. Fact 5 (preamble): the Anglo-American Committee paraphrases it, the COJS excerpt is a reprint. Fact 6 (Art. 2): the UN committee report discusses it, the Survey is a reprint. Fact 7 (Art. 25): UN committee yes, COJS reprint. Fact 10 (Art. 4): the UN committee passage is a footnote block quotation and the Survey a reprint, so no reader. Fact 11 (Art. 6): UN committee yes, Survey reprint. Facts 2, 3, 4, 8, 9 have two real readers (BBC, Rothschild Archive, IWM; The Times via FRUS; COJS description and UN committee; JTA and a US memorandum). Reprints confirm only that we copied accurately; I did not count them. [should-fix] Fixed by me: fact 4 omitted that the offer applied only where Britain was free to act without detriment to France, and its Commonweal quote was a reviewer's inference, now the reviewer's report of the exclusion; fact 6 dropped 'and the development of self-governing institutions'; fact 9 dropped the condition 'if economic absorptive capacity permits' and that 75,000 is 10,000 a year plus 25,000 refugees; answer said 'never called Palestine' (the sources say no province was named Palestine) and 'protected' the civil and religious rights (the text says nothing should prejudice them). [nit] Facts 0 and 1 are facts about the world with three independent sources; fact 8 relies on a League note read from an ECF scan; the Palquest and LOC pages were unreadable here (403). Missing counter: the White Paper's other conclusion (an independent Palestine within ten years) is not on this card. Strongest objections: Palestinian side, Articles 4 and 6 now present but the Mandate's silence on Arab national rights is stated only by IWM and the Rothschild Archive; Israeli side, none new.

citer.notes: Round two after the record rule. Answer re-split into 8 sentences, each tied to facts. Reworded 'never called Palestine' to 'no province was named Palestine' (fact 0), 'protected' to 'said nothing should prejudice' (fact 3), 'Sovereignty' to 'Rule ... as Mandatory' (facts 1, 5, 6). The sentence on Articles 4 and 6 is carried by facts 5, 10, 11 whose readers are thin (see skeptic); the sentences themselves say only what those facts say.
